claim: In humans and mice, double strand break (DSB) hotspot locations are determined by the DNA-binding specificity of the zinc finger array of the PRDM9 protein.
source: In humans and mice, and likely many other metazoan species, the primary determinant of hotspot locations is PRDM9 and the DNA-binding specificity of its Cys-2-His-2 Zinc Finger (ZF) array (Myers et al., 2010; Baudat et al., 2010; Parvanov et al., 2010; Baker et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Myers et al., 2010; Baudat et al., 2010; Parvanov et al., 2010; Baker et al., 2017).

claim: PRDM9 is rapidly evolving at residues in contact with DNA.
source: In humans and mice, double strand break (DSB) hotspot locations are determined by the DNA-binding specificity of the zinc finger array of the PRDM9 protein, which is rapidly evolving at residues in contact with DNA.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a known fact about PRDM9.

claim: PRDM9 binding on both homologs facilitates DSB repair.
source: Recent experimental work indicates that PRDM9 binding on both homologs facilitates DSB repair, and that the absence of sufficient symmetric binding disrupts meiosis.
evidence: Stated as a finding from recent experimental work.

claim: The absence of sufficient symmetric PRDM9 binding disrupts meiosis.
source: Recent experimental work indicates that PRDM9 binding on both homologs facilitates DSB repair, and that the absence of sufficient symmetric binding disrupts meiosis.
evidence: Stated as a finding from recent experimental work.

claim: The loss of a small number of strong binding sites leads to the use of a greater number of weaker ones.
source: We show that the loss of a small number of strong binding sites leads to the use of a greater number of weaker ones, resulting in a sharp reduction in symmetric binding and favoring new PRDM9 alleles that restore the use of a smaller set of strong binding sites.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The loss of strong binding sites results in a sharp reduction in symmetric binding.
source: We show that the loss of a small number of strong binding sites leads to the use of a greater number of weaker ones, resulting in a sharp reduction in symmetric binding and favoring new PRDM9 alleles that restore the use of a smaller set of strong binding sites.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The reduction in symmetric binding favors new PRDM9 alleles that restore the use of a smaller set of strong binding sites.
source: We show that the loss of a small number of strong binding sites leads to the use of a greater number of weaker ones, resulting in a sharp reduction in symmetric binding and favoring new PRDM9 alleles that restore the use of a smaller set of strong binding sites.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The advantage of new PRDM9 alleles is in limiting the number of binding sites used effectively, rather than in increasing net PRDM9 binding.
source: Our results therefore suggest that the advantage of new PRDM9 alleles is in limiting the number of binding sites used effectively, rather than in increasing net PRDM9 binding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model results.

claim: The evolutionary advantage of hotspots may have been to increase the efficiency of DSB repair and/or homolog pairing.
source: By extension, our model suggests that the evolutionary advantage of hotspots may have been to increase the efficiency of DSB repair and/or homolog pairing.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the model.

claim: Recombination is more uniformly spread across the genome in Drosophila.
source: Why recombination is concentrated in hotspots in some taxa, as opposed to being more uniformly spread across the genome, as in Drosophila (Manzano-Winkler et al., 2013; Smukowski Heil et al., 2015) or C. elegans (Kaur and Rockman, 2014; Bernstein and Rockman, 2016), remains unknown.
evidence: Supported by citations (Manzano-Winkler et al., 2013; Smukowski Heil et al., 2015).

claim: Recombination is more uniformly spread across the genome in C. elegans.
source: Why recombination is concentrated in hotspots in some taxa, as opposed to being more uniformly spread across the genome, as in Drosophila (Manzano-Winkler et al., 2013; Smukowski Heil et al., 2015) or C. elegans (Kaur and Rockman, 2014; Bernstein and Rockman, 2016), remains unknown.
evidence: Supported by citations (Kaur and Rockman, 2014; Bernstein and Rockman, 2016).

claim: PRDM9 binds to thousands of binding sites along the genome early in meiosis.
source: Early in meiosis, PRDM9 binds to thousands of binding sites along the genome (Grey et al., 2017; Parvanov et al., 2017), where its PR/SET domain catalyzes the formation of H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 marks on nearby histones (Hayashi et al., 2005; Grey et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2013; Eram et al., 2014; Powers et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations (Grey et al., 2017; Parvanov et al., 2017).

claim: The PR/SET domain of PRDM9 catalyzes the formation of H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 marks on nearby histones.
source: Early in meiosis, PRDM9 binds to thousands of binding sites along the genome (Grey et al., 2017; Parvanov et al., 2017), where its PR/SET domain catalyzes the formation of H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 marks on nearby histones (Hayashi et al., 2005; Grey et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2013; Eram et al., 2014; Powers et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Hayashi et al., 2005; Grey et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2013; Eram et al., 2014; Powers et al., 2016).

claim: H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 marks and protein interactions mediated by the PRDM9 KRAB domain play a role in bringing PRDM9-bound sites to the chromosomal axis.
source: These marks, and protein interactions mediated by the PRDM9 KRAB domain, play a role in bringing PRDM9-bound sites to the chromosomal axis, where the SPO11 protein catalyzes the formation of DSBs at a small subset (Imai et al., 2017; Parvanov et al., 2017; Diagouraga et al., 2018; Thibault-Sennett et al., 2018; Bhattacharyya et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Imai et al., 2017; Parvanov et al., 2017; Diagouraga et al., 2018; Thibault-Sennett et al., 2018; Bhattacharyya et al., 2019).

claim: SPO11 protein catalyzes the formation of DSBs at a small subset of PRDM9-bound sites at the chromosomal axis.
source: These marks, and protein interactions mediated by the PRDM9 KRAB domain, play a role in bringing PRDM9-bound sites to the chromosomal axis, where the SPO11 protein catalyzes the formation of DSBs at a small subset (Imai et al., 2017; Parvanov et al., 2017; Diagouraga et al., 2018; Thibault-Sennett et al., 2018; Bhattacharyya et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Imai et al., 2017; Parvanov et al., 2017; Diagouraga et al., 2018; Thibault-Sennett et al., 2018; Bhattacharyya et al., 2019).

claim: In species lacking PRDM9, recombination rates are increased near promoter-like features such as transcriptional start sites or CpG islands.
source: Whereas in species lacking PRDM9, such as canids, birds, fungi and plants, recombination rates are increased near promoter-like features, such as transcriptional start sites or CpG islands (Auton et al., 2013; Singhal et al., 2015; Lam and Keeney, 2015; Yelina et al., 2015) and the recombination landscape is conserved over tens of millions of years (Singhal et al., 2015; Lam and Keeney, 2015), in species that use PRDM9 to direct recombination, recombination rates are not elevated near such features and the recombination landscape is rapidly-evolving.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Auton et al., 2013; Singhal et al., 2015; Lam and Keeney, 2015; Yelina et al., 2015).

claim: The recombination landscape is conserved over tens of millions of years in species lacking PRDM9.
source: Whereas in species lacking PRDM9, such as canids, birds, fungi and plants, recombination rates are increased near promoter-like features, such as transcriptional start sites or CpG islands (Auton et al., 2013; Singhal et al., 2015; Lam and Keeney, 2015; Yelina et al., 2015) and the recombination landscape is conserved over tens of millions of years (Singhal et al., 2015; Lam and Keeney, 2015), in species that use PRDM9 to direct recombination, recombination rates are not elevated near such features and the recombination landscape is rapidly-evolving.
evidence: Supported by citations (Singhal et al., 2015; Lam and Keeney, 2015).

claim: In species that use PRDM9 to direct recombination, recombination rates are not elevated near promoter-like features.
source: Whereas in species lacking PRDM9, such as canids, birds, fungi and plants, recombination rates are increased near promoter-like features, such as transcriptional start sites or CpG islands (Auton et al., 2013; Singhal et al., 2015; Lam and Keeney, 2015; Yelina et al., 2015) and the recombination landscape is conserved over tens of millions of years (Singhal et al., 2015; Lam and Keeney, 2015), in species that use PRDM9 to direct recombination, recombination rates are not elevated near such features and the recombination landscape is rapidly-evolving.
evidence: Stated as a contrast to species lacking PRDM9.

claim: The recombination landscape is rapidly-evolving in species that use PRDM9 to direct recombination.
source: Whereas in species lacking PRDM9, such as canids, birds, fungi and plants, recombination rates are increased near promoter-like features, such as transcriptional start sites or CpG islands (Auton et al., 2013; Singhal et al., 2015; Lam and Keeney, 2015; Yelina et al., 2015) and the recombination landscape is conserved over tens of millions of years (Singhal et al., 2015; Lam and Keeney, 2015), in species that use PRDM9 to direct recombination, recombination rates are not elevated near such features and the recombination landscape is rapidly-evolving.
evidence: Stated as a contrast to species lacking PRDM9.

claim: Hotspots used in humans and chimpanzees show no more overlap than expected by chance.
source: Notably, the hotspots used in closely related species, such as humans and chimpanzees, or even different subspecies, show no more overlap than expected by chance (Ptak et al., 2004; Winckler et al., 2005; Auton et al., 2012; Brick et al., 2012; Stevison et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Ptak et al., 2004; Winckler et al., 2005; Auton et al., 2012; Brick et al., 2012; Stevison et al., 2016).

claim: Gene conversion leads to the under-transmission of hot alleles in a manner that is mathematically analogous to purifying selection against them.
source: When individuals are heterozygous for 'hot' and 'cold' alleles, defined as those more or less likely to experience a DSB during meiosis, GC leads to the under-transmission of hot alleles in a manner that is mathematically analogous to purifying selection against them (Nagylaki and Petes, 1982; Jeffreys and Neumann, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations (Nagylaki and Petes, 1982; Jeffreys and Neumann, 2002).

claim: Polymorphisms disrupting PRDM9 binding motifs within hotspots are over-transmitted.
source: This phenomenon is observed in the over-transmission of polymorphisms disrupting PRDM9 binding motifs within hotspots (Berg et al., 2011; Cole et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations (Berg et al., 2011; Cole et al., 2014).

claim: PRDM9 binding sites erode unusually rapidly in primate and rodent lineages.
source: this prediction too is met, in the unusually rapid erosion of PRDM9 binding sites in primate and rodent lineages (Myers et al., 2010; Baker et al., 2015; Smagulova et al., 2016; Spence and Song, 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Myers et al., 2010; Baker et al., 2015; Smagulova et al., 2016; Spence and Song, 2019).

claim: Variation in hotspot usage has been associated with different PRDM9 alleles in mice, humans and cattle.
source: Variation in hotspot usage has been associated with different PRDM9 alleles (i.e. with different amino acids at the DNA-binding residues of their ZFs) in mice, humans and cattle (Myers et al., 2010; Baudat et al., 2010; Parvanov et al., 2010; Berg et al., 2010; Kong et al., 2010; Berg et al., 2011; Fledel-Alon et al., 2011; Hinch et al., 2011; Sandor et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2015), and the experimental introduction of a PRDM9 allele with a novel ZF-array into mice reprograms the locations of hotspots (Davies et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Myers et al., 2010; Baudat et al., 2010; Parvanov et al., 2010; Berg et al., 2010; Kong et al., 2010; Berg et al., 2011; Fledel-Alon et al., 2011; Hinch et al., 2011; Sandor et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2015).

claim: The experimental introduction of a PRDM9 allele with a novel ZF-array into mice reprograms the locations of hotspots.
source: Variation in hotspot usage has been associated with different PRDM9 alleles (i.e. with different amino acids at the DNA-binding residues of their ZFs) in mice, humans and cattle (Myers et al., 2010; Baudat et al., 2010; Parvanov et al., 2010; Berg et al., 2010; Kong et al., 2010; Berg et al., 2011; Fledel-Alon et al., 2011; Hinch et al., 2011; Sandor et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2015), and the experimental introduction of a PRDM9 allele with a novel ZF-array into mice reprograms the locations of hotspots (Davies et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation (Davies et al., 2016).

claim: Strong signatures of positive selection on the DNA-binding residues of ZFs from PRDM9 genes suggest rapid turnover of PRDM9 binding specificity driven by recurrent selection for novel binding specificities.
source: Moreover, strong signatures of positive selection on the DNA-binding residues of ZFs from PRDM9 genes suggests a rapid turnover of PRDM9 binding specificity driven by recurrent selection for novel binding specificities (Oliver et al., 2009; Thomas et al., 2009; Myers et al., 2010; Buard et al., 2014; Baker et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Oliver et al., 2009; Thomas et al., 2009; Myers et al., 2010; Buard et al., 2014; Baker et al., 2017).

claim: PRDM9-bound sites appear to compete for DSBs.
source: PRDM9-bound sites appear to compete for DSBs (Diagouraga et al., 2018) and the number of DSBs formed per meiosis is tightly regulated independently of PRDM9 (Kauppi et al., 2013; Yamada et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation (Diagouraga et al., 2018).

claim: The number of DSBs formed per meiosis is tightly regulated independently of PRDM9.
source: PRDM9-bound sites appear to compete for DSBs (Diagouraga et al., 2018) and the number of DSBs formed per meiosis is tightly regulated independently of PRDM9 (Kauppi et al., 2013; Yamada et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations (Kauppi et al., 2013; Yamada et al., 2017).

claim: Similar numbers of DSBs form in PRDM9-/- mice.
source: Similar numbers of DSBs form even in PRDM9-/- mice (Hayashi et al., 2005; Brick et al., 2012; Mihola et al., 2019) and in a PRDM9-/- human female (Narasimhan et al., 2016); in both cases, the localization of DSB appear to 'default' to those found of species lacking PRDM9.
evidence: Supported by citations (Hayashi et al., 2005; Brick et al., 2012; Mihola et al., 2019).

claim: Similar numbers of DSBs form in a PRDM9-/- human female.
source: Similar numbers of DSBs form even in PRDM9-/- mice (Hayashi et al., 2005; Brick et al., 2012; Mihola et al., 2019) and in a PRDM9-/- human female (Narasimhan et al., 2016); in both cases, the localization of DSB appear to 'default' to those found of species lacking PRDM9.
evidence: Supported by citation (Narasimhan et al., 2016).

claim: In PRDM9-/- mice and humans, the localization of DSBs appears to 'default' to those found in species lacking PRDM9.
source: Similar numbers of DSBs form even in PRDM9-/- mice (Hayashi et al., 2005; Brick et al., 2012; Mihola et al., 2019) and in a PRDM9-/- human female (Narasimhan et al., 2016); in both cases, the localization of DSB appear to 'default' to those found of species lacking PRDM9.
evidence: Stated as an observation from the cited studies.

claim: PRDM9 binding sites compete for available PRDM9 molecules.
source: Importantly, PRDM9 binding sites themselves are known to compete for available PRDM9 molecules, such that the loss of binding sites may only weakly affect the number bound (Billings et al., 2013; Baker et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations (Billings et al., 2013; Baker et al., 2014).

claim: PRDM9 has been shown to play a role in DSB repair, mediated by its symmetric recruitment to the same loci on homologous chromosomes during meiosis.
source: In addition to localizing DSBs, PRDM9 has recently been shown to play a role in DSB repair, mediated by its symmetric recruitment to the same loci on homologous chromosomes during meiosis (Smagulova et al., 2016; Davies et al., 2016; Gregorova et al., 2018; Hinch et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2020; Mahgoub et al., 2020; Wells et al., 2020; Gergelits et al., 2021; Davies et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Smagulova et al., 2016; Davies et al., 2016; Gregorova et al., 2018; Hinch et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2020; Mahgoub et al., 2020; Wells et al., 2020; Gergelits et al., 2021; Davies et al., 2021).

claim: In sterile mouse hybrids, the PRDM9 allele of each parental subspecies preferentially binds to the non-parental background because the strongest PRDM9 binding sites corresponding to the alleles in each parental subspecies have been eroded.
source: In these sterile hybrids, the PRDM9 allele of each parental subspecies preferentially binds to the non-parental background, because the strongest PRDM9 binding sites corresponding to the alleles in each parental subspecies have been eroded.
evidence: Stated as an explanation for observations in sterile hybrids.

claim: Asymmetric PRDM9 binding in sterile hybrids leads to meiotic arrest in pachytene, associated with widespread delays in DSB repair, asynaptic chromosomes, and defects in homolog pairing.
source: The resulting asymmetric binding leads to meiotic arrest in pachytene, associated with widespread delays in DSB repair, asynaptic chromosomes, and defects in homolog pairing (Baker et al., 2015; Smagulova et al., 2016; Davies et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations (Baker et al., 2015; Smagulova et al., 2016; Davies et al., 2016).

claim: Restoring PRDM9 binding symmetry is sufficient to rescue the fertility of hybrids.
source: Restoring PRDM9 binding symmetry, either through the introduction of a novel PRDM9 allele with functioning binding sites in either parental subspecies (Davies et al., 2016; Davies et al., 2021) or by partially restoring the homozygosity of binding sites on the chromosomes most prone to asynapsis (Gregorova et al., 2018), is sufficient to rescue the fertility of hybrids.
evidence: Supported by citations (Davies et al., 2016; Davies et al., 2021; Gregorova et al., 2018).

claim: Fertility depends on having a small number of DSBs at sites symmetrically bound by PRDM9 on each chromosome.
source: These results indicate that fertility depends on having a small number of DSBs at sites symmetrically bound by PRDM9 (Gregorova et al., 2018) on each chromosome.
evidence: Supported by citation (Gregorova et al., 2018) and inference from the results.

claim: DSBs at asymmetrically-bound hotspots are more likely to experience delays in their repair.
source: Genome-wide analyses indicate that DSBs at asymmetrically-bound hotspots are more likely to experience delays in their repair (Hinch et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019), that they are less likely to result in COs, possibly due to this delay (Hinch et al., 2019), and that they are more likely to be resolved using the sister chromatid rather than the homologous chromosome as a template (Li et al., 2019; Gergelits et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations (Hinch et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019).

claim: DSBs at asymmetrically-bound hotspots are less likely to result in crossovers.
source: Genome-wide analyses indicate that DSBs at asymmetrically-bound hotspots are more likely to experience delays in their repair (Hinch et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019), that they are less likely to result in COs, possibly due to this delay (Hinch et al., 2019), and that they are more likely to be resolved using the sister chromatid rather than the homologous chromosome as a template (Li et al., 2019; Gergelits et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation (Hinch et al., 2019).

claim: DSBs at asymmetrically-bound hotspots are more likely to be resolved using the sister chromatid rather than the homologous chromosome as a template.
source: Genome-wide analyses indicate that DSBs at asymmetrically-bound hotspots are more likely to experience delays in their repair (Hinch et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019), that they are less likely to result in COs, possibly due to this delay (Hinch et al., 2019), and that they are more likely to be resolved using the sister chromatid rather than the homologous chromosome as a template (Li et al., 2019; Gergelits et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations (Li et al., 2019; Gergelits et al., 2021).

claim: ZCWPW1 is implicated in mediating efficient repair at symmetrically bound sites.
source: Recent work has further implicated the gene ZCWPW1 in mediating efficient repair at symmetrically bound sites (Huang et al., 2020; Mahgoub et al., 2020; Wells et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations (Huang et al., 2020; Mahgoub et al., 2020; Wells et al., 2020).

claim: The model assumes that the number of DSBs is regulated independently of PRDM9.
source: Based on this premise, we model the co-evolution of PRDM9 and its binding sites from first principles, assuming, as seems realistic, that: (i) the number of DSBs is regulated independently of PRDM9, (ii) PRDM9 binding is competitive between sites (i.e. the availability of PRDM9 is limiting), and (iii) fitness is a function of the probability that the smallest chromosome experiences some minimal number of DSBs at sites symmetrically bound by PRDM9.
evidence: This is an explicit assumption of the model.

claim: The model assumes that PRDM9 binding is competitive between sites.
source: Based on this premise, we model the co-evolution of PRDM9 and its binding sites from first principles, assuming, as seems realistic, that: (i) the number of DSBs is regulated independently of PRDM9, (ii) PRDM9 binding is competitive between sites (i.e. the availability of PRDM9 is limiting), and (iii) fitness is a function of the probability that the smallest chromosome experiences some minimal number of DSBs at sites symmetrically bound by PRDM9.
evidence: This is an explicit assumption of the model.

claim: The model assumes that fitness is a function of the probability that the smallest chromosome experiences some minimal number of DSBs at sites symmetrically bound by PRDM9.
source: Based on this premise, we model the co-evolution of PRDM9 and its binding sites from first principles, assuming, as seems realistic, that: (i) the number of DSBs is regulated independently of PRDM9, (ii) PRDM9 binding is competitive between sites (i.e. the availability of PRDM9 is limiting), and (iii) fitness is a function of the probability that the smallest chromosome experiences some minimal number of DSBs at sites symmetrically bound by PRDM9.
evidence: This is an explicit assumption of the model.

claim: The model describes PRDM9 binding during meiosis in terms of Michaelis-Menten kinetics.
source: The first describes PRDM9 binding during meiosis in terms of Michaelis-Menten kinetics, in which sites compete for binding their cognate PRDM9 proteins.
evidence: This is an explicit component of the model.

claim: In the model, sites compete for binding their cognate PRDM9 proteins.
source: The first describes PRDM9 binding during meiosis in terms of Michaelis-Menten kinetics, in which sites compete for binding their cognate PRDM9 proteins.
evidence: This is an explicit component of the model.

claim: The model considers only the smallest chromosome because fitness defects arising from asymmetry in PRDM9 binding should affect the smallest chromosomes first.
source: For simplicity, we consider only the smallest chromosome because fitness defects arising from asymmetry in PRDM9 binding should affect the smallest chromosomes first (assuming, as seems plausible, that they have fewer sites at which a symmetric DSB might be made).
evidence: This is an explicit simplification in the model with a stated rationale.

claim: Individual fitness is assumed to equal the probability of a symmetric DSB in a single meiosis.
source: Also for simplicity, we assume that individual fitness is equal to the probability of a symmetric DSB in a single meiosis.
evidence: This is an explicit simplification in the model.

claim: Mutations that destroy the ability of a site to bind to its cognate PRDM9 are introduced with probability μ per individual meiosis.
source: Lastly, we use a deterministic approximation to describe the erosion of binding sites over time (Figure 1D). Mutations that destroy the ability of a site to bind to its cognate PRDM9 are introduced with probability μ per individual meiosis and can fix in the population due to biased gene conversion.
evidence: This is an explicit component of the model.

claim: The fixation probability of mutations that destroy PRDM9 binding depends on rates at which the binding site experiences a DSB and of gene conversion.
source: Mutations that destroy the ability of a site to bind to its cognate PRDM9 are introduced with probability μ per individual meiosis and can fix in the population due to biased gene conversion. The fixation probability depends on rates at which the binding site experiences a DSB and of GC.
evidence: This is an explicit component of the model.

claim: Turnover time is inversely proportional to population size.
source: Turnover time is inversely proportional to population size (Figure 6B), because the increase in mutational input at binding sites and thus the rate at which they are lost are proportional to the population size (see Equation 11); other factors, such as the mutational input at PRDM9, have negligible effects by comparison (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the model shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The turnover time is shorter for strong hotspots than for weak ones.
source: The turnover time is shorter for strong hotspots than for weak ones (Figure 6B), because PRDM9 alleles with stronger hotspots enter the population with fewer hotspots (Figure 6A) and stronger hotspots experience more DSBs and are therefore lost faster.
evidence: This is a finding from the model shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Average PRDM9 diversity is expected to be greater in larger populations.
source: Consequently, average PRDM9 diversity is expected to be greater in larger populations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model dynamics.

claim: The cycling dynamics characteristic of PRDM9 evolution entails a substantial genetic load.
source: The cycling dynamics characteristic of PRDM9 evolution over much of the parameter space entails a substantial genetic load, i.e., an average fitness that is substantially lower than its optimal value (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding from the model shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Average fitness is greater in smaller populations than in larger ones.
source: Moreover, in contrast to the usual case, in this setting, average fitness is greater in smaller populations than in larger ones, as the number of hotspots – and thus the fitness associated with the predominant PRDM9 alleles when they fix and when they exit the population – is lower in larger populations than in smaller ones (Figures 5 and 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from the model shown in Figures 5 and 6A.

claim: Previous models assumed that the loss of PRDM9 binding sites leads to a reduction in the number of DSBs.
source: Previous models of PRDM9 evolution demonstrated how selection to maintain a given rate of recombination (e.g., for there to be at least one crossover per chromosome) can act as a countervailing force to the loss of hotspots through gene conversion, and ensure the persistence of hotspots (Ubeda and Wilkins, 2011; Latrille et al., 2017). These models were based on an assumption now believed to be incorrect, however: that the loss of PRDM9 binding sites leads to a reduction in the number of DSBs.
evidence: This is a statement about previous models with citations (Ubeda and Wilkins, 2011; Latrille et al., 2017).

claim: When hotspots are lost, PRDM9 simply binds elsewhere.
source: Since DSB formation is regulated independently of PRDM9 (Kauppi et al., 2013; Yamada et al., 2017; Brick et al., 2012; Mihola et al., 2019) and hotspots are thought to compete for binding (Diagouraga et al., 2018), it more plausible that when hotspots are lost, PRDM9 simply binds elsewhere.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited evidence (Kauppi et al., 2013; Yamada et al., 2017; Brick et al., 2012; Mihola et al., 2019; Diagouraga et al., 2018).

claim: In the model, the selection driving the evolution of the PRDM9 ZF arises from the requirement of symmetric binding in DSB repair.
source: In our model, the selection driving the evolution of the PRDM9 ZF arises from the requirement of symmetric binding in DSB repair, and thus from changes in the shape of its binding distribution over time, rather than from changes in net binding, as previously assumed.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the model.

claim: Strong hotspots are lost more rapidly than weak ones.
source: Strong hotspots are lost more rapidly than weak ones, resulting in a shift from a small number of strong binding sites to a larger number of weak binding sites over the lifespan of a PRDM9 allele.
evidence: This is a finding from the model.

claim: The shift from strong to weak binding sites entails a reduction in the number of symmetric DSBs.
source: Strong hotspots are lost more rapidly than weak ones, resulting in a shift from a small number of strong binding sites to a larger number of weak binding sites over the lifespan of a PRDM9 allele. This shift entails a reduction in the number of symmetric DSBs, and eventually selection in favor of a new PRDM9 allele.
evidence: This is a finding from the model.

claim: New PRDM9 alleles are favored because they redirect PRDM9 binding to a smaller proportion of the genome, making symmetric binding more likely.
source: They are favored because, in doing so, PRDM9 binding is redirected to a smaller proportion of the genome, and is therefore more likely to bind symmetrically.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model.

claim: The sites most likely to be symmetrically bound will also experience the highest rates of drive.
source: Accordingly, the sites most likely to be symmetrically bound will also experience the highest rates of drive, in accordance with empirical observations (Hinch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model supported by citation (Hinch et al., 2019).

claim: The loss of hotspots results in PRDM9 binding becoming more dispersed across the genome.
source: In our two-heat model, when hotspots are lost, PRDM9 binding shifts towards the more plentiful class of weak binding sites. Given a more realistic distribution of heats, we would similarly expect the loss of hotspots to result in PRDM9 binding becoming more dispersed across the genome.
evidence: This is an inference from the model extended to more realistic scenarios.

claim: The number of hotspots will increase over time as optimal binding motifs erode.
source: After the optimal binding motifs have eroded, most PRDM9 binding will plausibly shifts toward the next best and larger class of motifs, with one mismatch, and then those with two mismatches, and so on. This consideration suggests that the number of hotspots will increase over time (although the extent to which binding becomes more dispersed will depend on the degree to which PRDM9 binding is limiting).
evidence: This is an inference from the model extended to more realistic scenarios.

claim: The heat of observed hotspots should decrease over time.
source: This picture is in stark contrast with the previous understanding of the evolution of hotspots, namely, that gene conversion leads to a reduction in the number of hotspots over time. It further suggests that the heat of observed hotspots should decrease over time.
evidence: This is an inference from the model.

claim: In all species with a complete PRDM9 investigated to date, PRDM9 diversity appears to be high relative to other ZF genes, regardless of the effective population size.
source: In all species with a complete PRDM9 investigated to date, PRDM9 diversity appears to be high relative to other ZF genes, regardless of the effective population size (Buard et al., 2014; Vara et al., 2019; Alleva et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations (Buard et al., 2014; Vara et al., 2019; Alleva et al., 2021).

claim: The rate of mutation at the PRDM9 ZF array has been inferred to be quite high, with a ZF copy number change of ~0.3–20 x 10–5 per generation.
source: The rate of mutation at the PRDM9 ZF array has been inferred to be quite high, with a ZF copy number change of ~0.3–20 x 10–5 per generation (Jeffreys et al., 2013), as expected from its minisatellite nature.
evidence: Supported by citation (Jeffreys et al., 2013).

claim: Strong signatures of erosion at binding sites associated with PRDM9 alleles in several species seem indicative of a cycling dynamic.
source: The strong signatures of erosion at binding sites associated with PRDM9 alleles in several species (Myers et al., 2010; Smagulova et al., 2016; Hoge et al., 2023) seem indicative of a cycling dynamic.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited evidence (Myers et al., 2010; Smagulova et al., 2016; Hoge et al., 2023).

claim: Being heterozygote for a minor PRDM9 ZFs is protective against azoospermia in humans.
source: In turn, anecdotal evidence suggests that being heterozygote for a minor PRDM9 ZFs is protective against azoospermia in humans (Irie et al., 2009), and the high levels of PRDM9 diversity seen across species with very different effective population sizes might suggest that the dynamics are closer to expectations for strong hotspots.
evidence: Supported by citation (Irie et al., 2009).

claim: Most empirical manipulations that rescue fertility in otherwise sterile crosses of hybrid mice can be readily understood as restoring symmetric binding.
source: Most empirical manipulations that rescue fertility in otherwise sterile crosses of hybrid mice can be readily understood as restoring symmetric binding (Davies et al., 2016; Gregorova et al., 2018; Davies et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations (Davies et al., 2016; Gregorova et al., 2018; Davies et al., 2021).

claim: Fertility can be restored by increasing the expression of either PRDM9 allele present in sterile hybrids.
source: Two of these manipulations require more nuanced explanations, however: notably, why is it that fertility can be restored by either (i) increasing the expression of either PRDM9 allele present (Flachs et al., 2012), or by (ii) removing one allele but not the other, for example removing the B6 allele in a cross between B6 and PWD mice (Flachs et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation (Flachs et al., 2012).

claim: Fertility can be restored by removing one PRDM9 allele but not the other in sterile hybrids.
source: Two of these manipulations require more nuanced explanations, however: notably, why is it that fertility can be restored by either (i) increasing the expression of either PRDM9 allele present (Flachs et al., 2012), or by (ii) removing one allele but not the other, for example removing the B6 allele in a cross between B6 and PWD mice (Flachs et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation (Flachs et al., 2012).

claim: In sterile hybrids, available PRDM9 is being sequestered to the non-parental genetic background, where their strongest binding sites have not been eroded.
source: In the sterile hybrids, no sites experience a symmetric DSB on the smallest chromosome. Nonetheless, binding sites for both alleles occur on their respective parental backgrounds, as evidenced by their use in the parental mice. Why then are they not used in the hybrids? We suggest that the reason is because PRDM9 is limiting, and the available PRDM9 is being sequestered to the non-parental genetic background, where their strongest binding sites have not been eroded.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors.

claim: Increasing PRDM9 expression of either allele results in more PRDM9 binding at parental binding sites, allowing for symmetric binding.
source: Increasing PRDM9 expression of either allele results in more PRDM9 binding at parental binding sites, allowing for symmetric binding.
evidence: This is an explanation proposed by the authors based on the model.

claim: The evolutionary benefit of PRDM9 binding symmetrically plausibly stems from the preferentially use of the same loci on one chromosome for DSB initiation and, on the homologous chromosome, for DSB repair.
source: Given recent findings, the evolutionary benefit of PRDM9 binding symmetrically plausibly stems from the preferentially use of the same loci on one chromosome for DSB initiation and, on the homologous chromosome, for DSB repair (see Introduction).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on recent findings discussed in the Introduction.

claim: This strategy improves the efficacy of both homolog pairing and DSB repair, potentially by reducing the search space during homolog engagement and/or by increasing the accessibility of the loci for strand invasion and subsequent steps of repair.
source: This strategy improves the efficacy of both homolog pairing and DSB repair, potentially by reducing the search space during homolog engagement and/or by increasing the accessibility of the loci for strand invasion and subsequent steps of repair.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation.

claim: The advantage of hotspots may be to limit recombination to a small proportion of the genome.
source: Davies et al., 2016 hypothesized that by the same reasoning, the advantage of hotspots may be to limit recombination to a small proportion of the genome (in species that do not use PRDM9 but have hotspots, such as birds, as well as those that do; Singhal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from Davies et al., 2016 with supporting citation (Singhal et al., 2015).

claim: Taxa with DSB-independent mechanisms of homolog pairing, such as Drosophila or C. elegans, do not have hotspots.
source: In this regard, it is noteworthy that taxa with DSB-independent mechanisms of homolog pairing, such as Drosophila or C. elegans, do not have hotspots (Manzano-Winkler et al., 2013; Smukowski Heil et al., 2015; Kaur and Rockman, 2014; Bernstein and Rockman, 2016), whereas most species with DSB-dependent mechanisms, such as most yeast, plants or vertebrates, do (Auton et al., 2013; Singhal et al., 2015; Lam and Keeney, 2015; Yelina et al., 2015; Tock and Henderson, 2018; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations (Manzano-Winkler et al., 2013; Smukowski Heil et al., 2015; Kaur and Rockman, 2014; Bernstein and Rockman, 2016).

claim: Most species with DSB-dependent mechanisms of homolog pairing have hotspots.
source: In this regard, it is noteworthy that taxa with DSB-independent mechanisms of homolog pairing, such as Drosophila or C. elegans, do not have hotspots (Manzano-Winkler et al., 2013; Smukowski Heil et al., 2015; Kaur and Rockman, 2014; Bernstein and Rockman, 2016), whereas most species with DSB-dependent mechanisms, such as most yeast, plants or vertebrates, do (Auton et al., 2013; Singhal et al., 2015; Lam and Keeney, 2015; Yelina et al., 2015; Tock and Henderson, 2018; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations (Auton et al., 2013; Singhal et al., 2015; Lam and Keeney, 2015; Yelina et al., 2015; Tock and Henderson, 2018; Liu et al., 2019).

claim: PRDM9 arose prior to the common ancestor of animals and has since been repeatedly lost, including more than a dozen times across vertebrates.
source: PRDM9 arose prior to the common ancestor of animals and has since been repeatedly lost, including more than a dozen times across vertebrates (Baker et al., 2017; Cavassim et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations (Baker et al., 2017; Cavassim et al., 2022).

claim: In vertebrate lineages in which PRDM9 has been lost, recombination events are concentrated in hotspots that tend to be found associated with promoter-like features of the genome.
source: In vertebrate lineages in which PRDM9 has been lost, such as canids, birds or percomorph fish, as well as in PRDM9 knockout mice and rats, and to a minor degree in sterile mice hybrids, recombination events are concentrated in hotspots that tend to be found associated with promoter-like features of the genome, such as transcriptional start sites and/or CpG-islands (Brick et al., 2012; Auton et al., 2013; Singhal et al., 2015; Smagulova et al., 2016; Mihola et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations (Brick et al., 2012; Auton et al., 2013; Singhal et al., 2015; Smagulova et al., 2016; Mihola et al., 2021).

claim: The mechanism for localizing hotspots to promoter-like features is likely ancestral to the evolution of PRDM9's role in recombination.
source: Therefore, this mechanism for localizing hotspots is likely ancestral to the evolution of PRDM9's role in recombination, and is retained in the presence of PRDM9.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that this mechanism is found in lineages without PRDM9.

claim: The two mechanisms for localizing hotspots may be engaged in a tug of war, the outcome of which is more lopsided in mice and humans and more even in other species, such as snakes.
source: Indeed, recent work suggests that the two mechanisms may be engaged in a tug of war, the outcome of which is more lopsided in mice and humans and more even in other species, such as snakes (Hoge et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation (Hoge et al., 2023).

claim: PRDM9 may be favored when it further enhances the degree of symmetric recruitment of factors involved in both DSB initiation and DSB repair relative to that of default hotspots.
source: If species without PRDM9 also recruit factors involved in both DSB initiation and DSB repair on both homologs, then PRDM9 may be favored when it further enhances the degree of symmetric recruitment of such factors relative to that of default hotspots, that is when PRDM9-mediated hotspots are fewer and hotter than default hotspots given the same number of DSBs.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation.

claim: DSB heats measured by DMC1 ChIP-seq are higher in wild type than in PRDM9-/- mice.
source: In support of this possibility, DSB heats measured by DMC1 ChIP-seq are higher in wild type than in PRDM9-/- mice (Brick et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation (Brick et al., 2012).

claim: PRDM9 may enable the successful completion of meiosis with fewer DSBs.
source: If PRDM9 improves the efficiency of DSB-dependent homolog engagement, it may also enable the successful completion of meiosis with fewer DSBs—a potentially important secondary benefit, given that DSBs pose an inherent danger to cellular survival (Cooper et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation with supporting citation (Cooper et al., 2016).

claim: Not all strains of mice are sterile when PRDM9 is knocked out, and those which are tend to have fewer DSBs per meiosis.
source: Notably, not all strains of mice are sterile when PRDM9 is knocked out, and those which are tend to have fewer DSBs per meiosis (Mihola et al., 2019), which seems to support the hypothesis that PRDM9 may be especially important for the successful completion of meiosis with fewer DSBs.
evidence: Supported by citation (Mihola et al., 2019).
